passage: A month after the family had agreed the new schedule, they sat in the shop after closing with the tea kettle between them and the tally notebook open. Papa asked each person to say what was working. Parul said the Tuesday evening shift was fine but tiring. Sachin, Parul's brother, admitted the same slot clashed with his coaching class. Mother slid the notebook over: the daily sheets Parul filled from camp had made the evening tally match for the first time in years. They swapped, so Sachin took Saturday mornings and Parul took Tuesdays. Then Papa thanked each of them by name, for the counter, the sheets and the patience. Parul stacked the cups a little more lightly than usual. They wrote the next review on the calendar for a month ahead.

qa.q: Why did the Tuesday shift need to change?
qa.a: It clashed with Sachin's coaching class.

qa.q: What might Parul have felt when Papa thanked each person by name?
qa.a: Seen and valued, which makes the arrangement feel fair instead of a burden.

qa.q: What else could the family do to keep the arrangement fair, and why?
qa.a: Set the next review a month ahead, because exams and stock change and a regular check lets them adjust before resentment grows.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Sachin?
qa.a: A shift he did not choose had squeezed his coaching time, so the swap shows that his time matters too.

grounding: A month on, the family reviews the schedule, adjusts shifts and makes sure each person's effort is seen.

A month after the deal, Liam's family in Cork sat down after closing time at their fish-and-chip shop. The deal had been simple: Liam worked Friday and Saturday evenings, and on weekdays he went to his coding club.

His mum Esther had a notebook. "So. Is it working?"

"Fridays are fine," Liam said. "Saturdays I'm dead for Sunday homework."

His dad nodded. "And Tuesdays we're short. The delivery boy quit."

Esther wrote it down. "What if Liam swaps Saturday for Tuesday, just the early shift?"

Liam thought. "Tuesday club ends at five. I could be here by half past."

"And I'll do Saturdays," Esther said. "I didn't realise you were that tired."

"I didn't realise you were short on Tuesdays," Liam said. "Nobody said."

They shook hands on it, a little jokingly. It felt fairer than the first version.

qa.q: Which evenings did Liam work in the original deal?
How did Liam feel when Esther said she hadn't realised he was that tired?
qa.a: He probably felt seen and relieved, since the review brought his tiredness into the open.

qa.q: What else could the family do to keep the arrangement fair?
qa.a: They could agree to review it again after another month, since needs like the missing delivery boy can change.

qa.q: How might Esther see the review?
qa.a: Esther seems glad she asked, because it revealed problems on both sides that no one had mentioned.

grounding: Shows a student and family reviewing a work schedule after a month, adjusting shifts and making sure each person's effort is seen so the arrangement stays fair.

subtype: Approach: reviewing the compromise after a month [Revision]

The school counsellor's room was small, with a window facing the basketball court. Tushar sat beside his mother, Mahima, who had come straight from their tailoring shop.

A month ago, in this room, they'd agreed: Tushar would help with alterations on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday, and keep Tuesday and Thursday for his debate club.

"How is it going?" the counsellor asked.

"Wednesday is too much," Tushar said. "I have tests on Thursday mornings."

Mahima nodded. "And Saturdays he works harder than anyone. I never told him that." She turned to him. "You finished the whole wedding order last week."

Tushar looked at his shoes, pleased.

They shifted Wednesday to Sunday morning. The counsellor wrote the new plan on a sheet and gave them each a copy. "Let's check again in a month."

On the way out, Mahima squeezed his shoulder.

qa.q: Which days did Tushar keep for debate club?
How did Tushar feel when his mother praised his Saturday work?
qa.a: He felt pleased and appreciated, looking at his shoes a little shyly.

qa.q: What else could the counsellor suggest for the next review?
qa.a: The counsellor could ask both to note any week that felt too heavy, so problems are clear before the next meeting.

qa.q: How does the review look to Mahima?
qa.a: Mahima seems grateful for the chance to say what she had never told him, and willing to shift the days for his tests.

grounding: Shows a student and parent reviewing a shop-and-club schedule after a month, adjusting days and confirming each person's effort is seen.
